lessonPassage:
Newton's Second Law states that 'the net force acting on an object equals the rate of change of its momentum with respect to time.' Mathematically, this means the object's acceleration is directly proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to its mass.

F = m x a
F: Net force (Newtons, N)  |  m: Mass (kilograms, kg)  |  a: Acceleration (m/s2)

Force-Acceleration: The greater the force applied, the greater the acceleration — always in the same direction as the force.
Mass-Acceleration: Objects with greater mass require more force to achieve the same acceleration.

questions.questionText: Based on the definition at the start of the passage, what does 'net force acting on an object' equal?
options: The product of the object's mass and its velocity
The rate of change of the object's momentum with respect to time
The square of the speed divided by time
The direction of motion when external forces act on the object
questions.explanation: According to the passage: net force = rate of change of momentum with respect to time.

questions.questionText: According to the passage, what is the correct mathematical relationship between acceleration, force, and mass?
options: Proportional to mass and inversely proportional to force
Proportional to both force and mass
Inversely proportional to both force and mass
Proportional to force and inversely proportional to mass
questions.explanation: The passage states: acceleration is directly proportional to force and inversely proportional to mass.

questions.questionText: In the equation F = m x a, what unit is used to measure force?
options: Kilogram (kg)
Newton (N)
Meter per second squared (m/s2)
Joule (J)
questions.explanation: The passage defines F as net force measured in Newtons (N).

questions.questionText: According to the passage, what happens to acceleration when a greater force is applied to an object?
options: Acceleration decreases
Acceleration stays the same
Acceleration increases in the same direction as the force
Acceleration increases in the opposite direction of the force
questions.explanation: The passage states: the greater the force, the greater the acceleration — always in the same direction.

questions.questionText: Based on the passage, why do objects with greater mass require more force to accelerate?
options: Because force is proportional to mass
Because acceleration is inversely proportional to mass
Because momentum does not change with mass
Because velocity is constant regardless of mass
questions.explanation: The passage states acceleration is inversely proportional to mass, so more mass means more force is needed for the same acceleration.
